newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Serb witness had 'motive for fabrication' - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Serb witness had 'motive for fabrication' - lawyer.

text.p: A prosecution witness at the U.N. criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia had a "motive for fabrication", a defence lawyer claimed on Monday.

Mirko Babic, a 63-year-old Serb and former inmate at Celebici detention camp, was testifying before The Hague court in the trial of Moslems Hazim Delic, Esad Landzo and Zejnil Delalic and Croat camp commander Zdravko "Pavo" Mucic.
The four are charged with allegedly committing war crimes at the camp in Konjic, central Bosnia in 1992. All deny the charges.
Mucic, 41, and Delalic, 48, are accused of command responsibility for atrocities at the camp in 1992 including at least 14 murders and a catalogue of torture, rape and sexual assault.
Deputy camp commander Delic, 32, is also charged with command responsibility and, along with 24-year-old camp guard Landzo, of actually taking part in torture, rapes and killings.

But lawyer Cynthia White McMurrey, defending Landzo, said discrepancies between Babic's testimony to the tribunal last week and his initial statement to U.N. investigators in February 1996 showed a "motive for fabrication".
"The (February 1996 statement) was dramatic and exaggerated and not at all related to what he said on Wednesday," McMurrey told the court.
Babic testified last week that in July 1992 Landzo took him from the hangar where prisoners were held and told him to bare his leg before dousing it with petrol and setting it alight.

Turning to the same account in Babic's statement to U.N. investigators, McMurrey said: "This story is not what you said on February 20...there, he ripped your pants off with a knife and you were standing naked...there is a great difference."
Comparing Babic's accounts of other incidents McMurrey repeatedly asked "Were you lying then or are you lying now?"

She said as an organiser of the Serb resistance in his home village of Bjeloviccina near Konjic, he had no longer been working as a forester when the war started as he claimed but had been dismissed for taking bribes.
Babic, a known drinker, had also been dismissed from another timber industry post for drinking on the job, she alleged.
But Babic vigorously denied the allegations.
"That is just propaganda, lies and insults against me," he said.
After a gruelling three-hour cross-examination, Babic asked if he could briefly stand down from the witness box, pleading loss of memory.
"It's been five years...I am losing it out of my sight because I do not want to talk about it any more," he said.
